props.title: Six rules that hold the work together.

principles.title: Controlled complexity
principles.body: Depth is engineered, never improvised. Systems hold weight without leaking it to the surface.
principles.practice: Depth lives in the model and its boundaries. The surface shows only what the moment needs.

principles.title: Interfaces before noise
principles.body: A surface should resolve intent in a single read. Everything that does not serve clarity is removed.
principles.practice: A view resolves intent in a single read. Anything that does not help someone decide or act is removed.

principles.title: Motion with purpose
principles.body: Movement carries meaning — state, direction, hierarchy. Nothing moves to decorate.
principles.practice: Every transition reports state, direction or hierarchy. If a movement only decorates, it goes.

principles.title: Architecture that can expand
principles.body: Foundations are laid for systems that have not been announced yet. Growth is a property, not a rewrite.
principles.practice: Foundations are laid for what is not yet announced, so growth is an addition rather than a rewrite.

principles.title: Reveal only what is needed
principles.body: Access is scoped. Information surfaces by role, by context, by intent — never by default.
principles.practice: Information is scoped by role, context and intent before it ever reaches a screen.

principles.title: Production-minded prototypes
principles.body: Fast iteration on foundations that are already built to survive contact with real operations.
principles.practice: Early versions sit on foundations that can survive real use, so a prototype is a first release, not a throwaway.

terms.cookie: A small note a website asks your browser to keep and send back with later requests. This site’s own code sets none.
terms.session storage: A small store in your browser that belongs to one tab. The browser clears it when the tab closes.
terms.local storage: A store in your browser that stays until it is cleared. This site does not use it.
terms.IP address: The network address your connection appears to come from. Every website you visit receives it, because it is how a reply finds its way back.
terms.request log: A record a web server keeps of the requests it receives: usually the time, the address asked for and the sender’s IP address.
terms.third party: Someone other than you and the company: here, the services your browser is asked to contact so that the page can be shown.
terms.mail link: A link that opens your own email app with a message already started. Your email app, not this site, sends it.
terms.static site: A website made of ready-made files. It has no database and no accounts; the browser does the work of showing it.
terms.Google Fonts: A service that serves typefaces to websites. Using it means your browser contacts Google’s font servers.
terms.assistive technology: Software or devices that help people use a computer, such as screen readers, switch controls or magnifiers.
terms.screen reader: Software that reads what is on screen aloud, or shows it on a braille display.
terms.reduced motion: A setting in your device that asks websites to use less animation.
terms.WCAG: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: a widely used international standard for accessible web content.
terms.axe-core: An open-source engine that tests a page against accessibility rules automatically.
terms.canvas: A part of a web page that a script draws on. The animated backgrounds on this site are canvases.
terms.personal data: Information that identifies you or could be used to identify you, such as your name, your email address or your IP address.
terms.hosting: The service that stores the site’s files and delivers them to visitors’ browsers.
terms.retention period: How long a piece of information is kept before it is deleted.
terms.cache: A copy of something your browser keeps so it does not have to fetch it again, such as a font file or a script. It is the browser’s own store, outside the site’s code.
terms.browser history: The list of pages your browser remembers you visited. It is kept by your browser on your device, not by the site.
terms.VPN: A service that sends your connection through another network, so websites see that network’s address instead of yours.
terms.robots file: A plain file at the root of a site (robots.txt) that tells automated visitors which parts to leave alone.
terms.user-agent: The short description of itself that a browser or tool sends with every request, such as its name and version.
terms.redirect: An instruction that sends a visitor from one address to another.
terms.client-rendered: A site whose pages are assembled by JavaScript in your browser rather than delivered as finished pages.
terms.landmark: A named region of a page, such as the header, the navigation or the main content, that assistive technology can jump between.
terms.focus ring: The outline that shows which control the keyboard is on.
terms.contrast ratio: How much lighter or darker text is than its background, as a number from 1:1 to 21:1. Higher is easier to read.
terms.screen magnifier: Software that enlarges part of the screen.
terms.voice control: Software that lets people operate a computer by speaking, often by saying the names of the buttons and links they can see.
terms.switch control: A way of operating a computer with one or two buttons, for people who cannot use a keyboard or a pointer.
terms.ARIA: A set of attributes that tell assistive technology the role and state of page elements when plain HTML cannot.
terms.reflow: Text and layout rearranging themselves to fit a narrow window or a large text size, instead of scrolling sideways.
terms.data-protection authority: A public body in a country that oversees how personal data is handled and hears complaints about it.
terms.infringement: Using something protected by copyright or a trademark in a way the owner has not allowed and the law does not permit.
terms.licence: Permission, with conditions, to use something that belongs to someone else.
terms.warranty: A promise that something is as described or will work as stated.
terms.open source: Software whose source code is published under a licence that lets other people use and change it.
terms.browser tool: One of the small utilities in the Resources section, such as the contrast checker. It runs in your browser and sends nothing anywhere.

Please do not post the details publicly, or send them to anyone else, before the company has had a fair chance to fix the problem.

list: Use only your own browser, device and, where one is needed, your own account on a service. The site has no accounts.
Do not access, change or delete anything that belongs to someone else.
Do not run automated scans at a rate that could slow the site for others.
Stop as soon as you have shown there is a problem. Do not look for more.

props.intro: The pager goes off. Read each runbook one block at a time, and watch the clock that counts the time it takes to read, until you reach the first thing that actually does something.
props.incident: Alert: checkout error rate is above its threshold. Customers report that paying fails with a generic error.

blocks.text: Checkout is the service that sits between the storefront and the payment provider. It was built in two phases: the first handled card payments, the second added wallet payments. It uses a queue to hand finished orders on to fulfilment, and a cache that holds each visitor’s basket and session for fifteen minutes.

The service has three dependencies: the payment provider’s interface, the session cache and the orders database. Each has its own timeout, set in the settings file and described in the architecture document, which also explains why the timeouts differ.

Historically, outages of this kind have come from one of three places: the payment provider having a bad period, the cache running out of memory after a busy sale, or a release that changed one of the settings without anyone noticing it would affect checkout.
Work out which of the three is failing before you change anything.
Open the Checkout dependencies dashboard and compare the three error lines.
If the payment line is the highest, go to the section on provider outages. If the cache line is, go to the section on the cache. If neither, look at recent releases.
Open the provider’s status page and read the latest message.
Open the Checkout dependencies dashboard. Look at the three error lines.
Which line is highest? Payment → step 3. Cache → step 5. Neither → step 7.
Open the payment provider’s status page. Is it reporting a problem?
If yes: switch the storefront banner on (“Payments are slow; please try again shortly”), post in the incident channel, and stop. Nothing on our side will fix it.
Cache: check its memory graph. Above 90%? Run the “clear sessions” command (below) once. Expect the error line to fall within two minutes.
Not recovered after two minutes: page the second contact (see Escalation).
Neither: open the release list. Was anything released in the last two hours? If yes, roll it back using the rollback card.

props.note: The two runbooks are invented for the demonstration. Reading time is counted from their actual words at about 220 words a minute; a person woken at night reads more slowly.

props.intro: Three checks start on. Turn others on and off, and point at a problem for the check that usually finds it.

checks.blurb: Reads the code without running it.

checks.name: Unit tests
checks.blurb: Runs small pieces of logic in isolation.

checks.name: Integration tests
checks.blurb: Runs several parts together, with a real database or interface.

checks.name: End to end
checks.blurb: Drives the whole thing in a real browser.

checks.blurb: Tests pages against accessibility rules automatically.

checks.name: Real use
checks.blurb: A person using it, with a keyboard, a screen reader or a slow phone.

problems.text: A misspelt variable, or a missing import
problems.note: Static checks find these in seconds, before anything runs. It is the cheapest check there is.

problems.text: A calculation that is wrong for one input
problems.note: Unit tests are made for this: a small piece of logic, many inputs, exact answers.

problems.text: Two parts that each work but do not fit together
problems.note: Only tests that run the parts together can see this. Unit tests pass while the system fails.

problems.text: A button that does nothing in a real browser
problems.note: The page loads and the code is fine, but the click never arrives. A browser test, or a person, finds it.

problems.text: A control a screen reader cannot name
problems.note: Scans find missing names reliably. Whether the name makes sense takes a person.

problems.text: A menu that cannot be reached by keyboard
problems.note: Scans see only part of it. Walking through with the Tab key finds the rest.

problems.text: A page that crawls on a modest phone
problems.note: A fast development machine hides this. Measure on the device your slowest visitors use.

problems.text: A request that is processed twice
problems.note: You have to send it twice, at the awkward moment, to see it. Few teams think to; the guide on idempotency explains how.

props.note: The grid records judgement, not measurement. It is what experience says each kind of check is good at, and it is not exhaustive.

props.title: Six patterns, two at a time.
props.intro: Choose any two. Every row compares them: how they work, how soon the other side knows, how tightly they tie the systems together, and what each does when the other end is down.

patterns.name: Request and reply
patterns.how: One system asks the other directly and waits for the answer.
patterns.coupling: Tight: the caller needs the other side to be up and to keep its promises.
patterns.fails: The call fails. The caller must decide whether to retry, queue it or show an error.
patterns.effort: Moderate: a contract, authentication, timeouts and retries.
patterns.use: The answer is needed now, to carry on.
patterns.avoid: The other side is slow or unreliable, and the answer is not needed straight away.

patterns.name: Webhooks
patterns.how: The system where something happened sends a message to an address the other side provides.
patterns.coupling: Looser: the sender does not wait. The receiver must accept messages and reply quickly.
patterns.fails: The sender retries for a while and then gives up. Messages may arrive twice, late or out of order.
patterns.effort: Moderate: signatures, repeat-safe handling and a way to replay what was missed.
patterns.use: The other side needs to react soon after something happens.
patterns.avoid: You cannot receive requests from outside, or you need guaranteed order.

patterns.name: Polling
patterns.how: One side asks again and again whether anything has changed.
patterns.speed: As soon as the next poll. Frequent polling has a cost.
patterns.coupling: Loose: the other side needs to offer nothing special.
patterns.fails: A missed poll is caught by the next one. Easy to reason about.
patterns.effort: Low, but you must define exactly what “changed since” means.
patterns.use: The other side offers no push, and a delay of minutes is fine.
patterns.avoid: Freshness matters, or there are very many things to check.

patterns.name: Files on a schedule
patterns.how: One side writes a file, such as a spreadsheet or a CSV, and the other collects and loads it at set times.
patterns.speed: Hours, usually: whenever the batch runs.
patterns.coupling: Loose in time, tight in format: both must agree exactly on the file.
patterns.fails: A bad or missing file stops the batch, and is often found late.
patterns.effort: Low to build, higher to make dependable: validation, naming and reruns.
patterns.use: The other system only speaks files, or volumes are large and a delay is acceptable.
patterns.avoid: People are waiting on the result, or the format changes often.

patterns.name: Queue or message bus
patterns.how: Messages go to a broker that holds them until a consumer is ready for them.
patterns.speed: Seconds, even when the other side is busy.
patterns.coupling: Loose: producer and consumer never need to be up at the same time.
patterns.fails: Messages wait. Bad messages need handling. Consumers must cope with repeats.
patterns.effort: Higher: run a broker, design the messages, watch the backlog.
patterns.use: Bursts, many consumers, or a receiver that must never be overwhelmed.
patterns.avoid: A single simple call would do. The broker is another system to run.

patterns.name: A shared database
patterns.how: Both systems read and write the same tables.
patterns.coupling: The tightest of all: every change to the tables is felt by both.
patterns.fails: One system’s bad write damages the other. Every change has to be coordinated.
patterns.effort: Low at first and high ever after.
patterns.use: Rarely. Perhaps a read-only copy kept just for reporting.
patterns.avoid: Almost always. It looks easy, and it is how many systems become impossible to change.

props.note: General reference written for this site. It is not a recommendation for any particular system, and every real case has details that tip the balance.
